title: Verb + -ing forms and infinitives 1
subtitle: I resented Tom winning the prize.
summary: Choose between object + -ing and possessive + -ing, use the right preposition before an -ing form, and pick -ing or a bare infinitive after see, hear and make.

lesson.heading: Object + -ing or possessive + -ing
lesson.text: Some verbs can be followed either by an **object + -ing** or by a **possessive + -ing** with a similar meaning, although the possessive form is usually rather formal. We only use a possessive to talk about a person or a group of people.

examples.note: more formally I resented Tom's winning the prize.
more formally Mia recalled his buying the book.

examples.text: I remember **the horse winning** the race.

lesson.note: '(dis)liking' verbs: detest, (dis)approve of, (dis)like, hate, love, object to. 'thinking' verbs: forget, imagine, remember, think of.

lesson.heading: to + -ing, where to is a preposition
lesson.text: After some verbs **to** is a preposition, not part of an infinitive, so an **-ing** form follows. These verbs can also be followed by *to* + a noun phrase.

examples.note: also She confessed to the crime.

examples.text: You don't object **to working** late tonight, do you?
examples.note: also You don't object to the work, do you?

lesson.note: Also: adapt, adjust, admit, look forward, own up, resort.

lesson.heading: Other prepositions + -ing
rows: begin, close, end, finish (off / up), open, start (off / out)
Can you begin by cleaning the floors, and then do the windows?
concentrate, count, depend, focus, insist, rely
Clare insisted on (Jack) wearing a suit to the party.
approve, hear, know, speak, talk, tell
Have you ever heard of (anyone) getting arrested for gossiping before?
deter, discourage, keep, prevent, prohibit, stop
The noise from next door prevented me from sleeping.

lesson.heading: -ing or bare infinitive after feel, hear, notice, observe, overhear, see, watch

left.label: -ing = an action in progress, not seen from start to finish
examples: I saw them **playing** football from my window.
I was able to watch them **building** the new car park from my office window.

right.label: bare infinitive = a completed action, watched all the way through
examples: I watched him **climb** through the window, and then I called the police.

lesson.heading: dare and help
lesson.text: After **dare** and **help** we can use either a bare infinitive or a to-infinitive. But when *dare* has an **object**, only a to-infinitive is possible.

examples.text: I was angry with him, but I didn't dare **(to) say** anything.
We hope the Twitter campaign will help **(to) raise** awareness of the problem.
I dared him **to cross** the river.
examples.wrong: I dared him cross the river

lesson.heading: have, let and make
lesson.text: After **have**, **let** and **make** we use an object + **bare infinitive**, never a to-infinitive.

examples.text: His exam results might make him **work** harder.
examples.wrong: might make him to work harder

examples.text: I had Irena **clean up** her bedroom before I let her **go** out to play.

lesson.text: A bare infinitive after see, hear or watch says the whole event happened and you followed it through; an -ing form says you caught it in the middle.

exercises.prompt: More formal version: we don't approve of the ___ locating the factory so close to houses.
exercises.explanation: approve of is a '(dis)liking' verb, so a possessive + -ing is possible - and more formal.

exercises.prompt: More formal version: it is difficult to imagine ___ accepting the decision without any objection.
exercises.explanation: imagine is a 'thinking' verb: him accepting or, more formally, his accepting.

exercises.prompt: I heard the tyre ___ and then the lorry skidded across the road.
exercises.explanation: A single, short, completed event takes the bare infinitive.

exercises.statement: I watched him climb through the window, and then I called the police.
exercises.explanation: Correct. The bare infinitive shows that I watched the whole action from start to finish.

exercises.prompt: Match the beginnings and endings. Watch out for the object each verb needs.

pairs.left: When Lana thought of going on the roller-coaster it made ...
The new course is intended to help ...
Scientists hope the new drug will help ...
We didn't agree with the decision, but we didn't dare ...
The dial on the left lets ...
pairs.right: you control the speed of the fan.

exercises.prompt: Carl noticed someone ___ him from an upstairs window.
exercises.explanation: The -ing form fits: the watching was already going on, so Carl didn't see the whole event.

exercises.prompt: In a survey, 65% of dentists ___ mistakes in treating patients.
exercises.explanation: own up to + -ing: here to is a preposition, so making follows.

exercises.statement: I have always detested the dog's jumping up at me when I visit them.
exercises.explanation: I have always detested the dog jumping up at me. We only use a possessive + -ing for a person or a group of people.

exercises.prompt: I would like to ___ the main points of my talk.
exercises.explanation: end, begin, start and finish take by + -ing.

exercises.statement: His exam results might make him to work harder.
exercises.explanation: His exam results might make him work harder. After have, let and make we use a bare infinitive.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order. Remember what happens to dare when it has an object.
exercises.answer: I dared him to cross the river
exercises.explanation: With an object, dare takes only a to-infinitive: I dared him to cross - not ~~I dared him cross~~.
